doc.title: Derek Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

chapter: The Tonight Show and famous accompaniments
title: Sinatra and Placido Domingo; transposing on the spot
summary: Stories of Sinatra's arpeggio cue and Domingo's orchestra transposing up a minor third.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: Well I played the hell out of it. And I listed that on my resume — played with Pavarotti. But I mean all those guys over the years, I played with everybody — Frank Sinatra. Frank was between conductors and he’s had a pianist with him, a guy called Bill Miller, forever. They’re buddies all their lives. Well, he didn’t like the conductor so they elevated Bill Miller to be the conductor, and they said well we need a pianist, so get Derek in for this weekend. So I came down to Atlantic City to play, and so Frank is kind of older now, and he takes time in between things. And I’m kind of nervous see, I don’t trust the conductor and I’m thinking who am I going to get my cues from? But anyway, the tune comes up and it’s a piano arpeggio or something. So I give him the arpeggio. Frank stops, and he comes over to the piano and he’s got a drink, and he takes a drink, and he starts telling a story to the audience. It’s funny, and he has a drink and it’s the last show. And so he stops. So I give him the arpeggio again, you know. He comes back to the piano and takes another drink and he tells another story. And I’m really getting uptight here. So I give him another arpeggio. And he turns around to me and he deliberately says, “it’s okay, kid, you don’t have to hit me with a truck.” I said okay, I didn’t know what he had got. But in that time I worked with all these guys — Placido Domingo, they all came in and you just read the music. And I remember Placido, with a big orchestra, and you know he’s got a wonderful set of pipes and a marvelous voice. He says “don’t like that, take you up a minor third.” And this big orchestra. And nobody batted an eyelid. Everybody went straight into it and I have the piano part, I go woops!
No kidding. You mean the orchestra transposed it?
Absolutely. And not a word was said. Nobody complained — boom — straight into it.
I have never heard of that.
That’s not usually a skill that most people have.

That happened to us one time at Indiana University. We were playing a piece, the conductor said, “not exciting enough.” He said, “transpose up a minor third.” And he said, “next rehearsal, one of two things. If you can do it by ear, do it. If you can’t I want it written out on your own part. But when I call that modulation, it better be there.”
